first_impression.reaction: I googled this because James's sister offered to 'marry us' and we're also still deciding whether the legal bit happens in Sydney or overseas. First paragraph: it's set by law, there are four types, done. Second paragraph flags that overseas changes the answer. No fairytale language, no selling. That earned a proper read.

journey.quote: The person at the front of the ceremony is the one who makes it legal, so it pays to know which type yours is and how to check. If your celebration is overseas, the answer changes again.
journey.reaction: Straight to the two things I actually care about. Good sign.

journey.quote: The two Commonwealth types share one regulator and one register, which is why they are sometimes grouped as a single type, with three groups in all.
journey.reaction: You just told me four types, now it's three groups. I had to read it twice. I don't need the taxonomy debate, I need to know which one marries me.

journey.quote: There are over 10,000 of them in Australia.
journey.reaction: The four sub-sections are accurate but read like the government site. I skimmed most of this until 'How the types differ in practice'.

journey.section: Can a friend or family member marry you?
journey.quote: If a sibling or close friend is set on it, raise it well over a year before the wedding, because the notice must also reach the celebrant at least one month before the day.
journey.reaction: This is exactly our situation and we're about 14 months out, so we're basically already late. Useful, specific, and saves an awkward conversation later.

journey.section: Can a friend or family member marry you?
journey.quote: Most couples keep it simpler. Book an authorised celebrant for the marriage itself, and ask your celebrant how a friend or family member can take part in the ceremony, whether through a reading, a welcome or a few words of their own.
journey.reaction: Honest trade-off without telling us off. This is the bit I'll send James so he can raise it with his sister.

journey.section: How to check your celebrant is authorised
journey.quote: Check before you pay a deposit. It takes a few minutes on the official register.
journey.reaction: Practical. As a lawyer I like being told how to verify rather than being asked to trust.

journey.quote: Plan the signing into the run sheet. If an error on a certificate is found after the ceremony, it can be corrected only while the couple and witnesses are still present.
journey.reaction: That's an insider detail. The kind of thing that goes wrong on the day with no one accountable. Exactly what I want someone to have thought about.

journey.section: How do you become a marriage celebrant?
journey.quote: The Registrar of Marriage Celebrants must be satisfied that the applicant is 18 or over, holds the relevant qualifications or skills and is a fit and proper person.
journey.reaction: I already read this in the friend section. Not for me, so I skipped the rest.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Not your Australian celebrant, at least not legally.
journey.reaction: Clear answer, then two paths laid out side by side. This is the section that actually helps us decide.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments for the celebration abroad as your single point of contact, in your time zone and quoting in AUD, while the legal ceremony stays with you and your celebrant: speak with [Wedded Concierge]
journey.reaction: AUD quotes and one point of contact speak to my worries. But 'stays with you and your celebrant' only fits the marry-at-home path. If we marry legally abroad there is no Australian celebrant, so who handles that? And if we marry in Sydney first, does the Advisor plan around that date or do we juggle it?

journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing up front addresses the hidden-cost fear. Calm close, not a hard sell.

unanswered_questions: If we marry legally abroad, does the Wedded Advisor help with the destination's paperwork and local officiant, or is that entirely on us?
If we marry legally in Sydney first, does the Wedded Advisor plan the overseas celebration around that date, or do we coordinate the two ourselves?
Can a celebrant we choose in Australia still lead a symbolic ceremony at the overseas celebration, and does the Advisor organise that?
Have you planned a wedding that split the legal ceremony at home from the celebration abroad, and can we see it (venue and date)?
would_share_with: James: the 'Can a friend or family member marry you?' section, so he can talk to his sister about the timeline before she starts a Certificate IV
Mum and Dad (contributing): the two overseas paths, so they understand where the legal ceremony might happen

cta_reaction.quote: When the legal side is settled, [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=who-can-perform-a-marriage&utm_content=primary) can take on the celebration.
cta_reaction.why: Low-pressure and honest about where they stop, which I respect. But this is a legal explainer, and I enquire after a few posts plus a real wedding. I'd click through to look around, not to fill in a form yet.

top_3_changes: In 'Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?', rewrite 'while the legal ceremony stays with you and your celebrant' so it also covers the marry-legally-abroad path (where there is no Australian celebrant), and say plainly whether the Wedded Advisor plans the celebration around an Australian legal date or the couple coordinates the two.

Fold 'How do you become a marriage celebrant?' into 'Can a friend or family member marry you?'. It repeats the age, qualification and fit-and-proper criteria already given there, and readers like me skip it.

After the two overseas paths, link a real Wedded Wonderland wedding (venue and date) where the couple married legally at home and celebrated abroad. That is the proof that would move me from reading to enquiring.
